name: snow-1855-water-intakes-and-tidal-limit
description: Three Thames sites named in Snow 1855. Coordinates are of the landmarks he names, geocoded from OpenStreetMap via Nominatim; the works themselves are not surveyed here.

properties.name: Southwark and Vauxhall · Thames at Battersea Fields
properties.snow_says: The water works at London Bridge were abolished, and the united company derived their supply from the Thames at Battersea Fields, about half a mile above Vauxhall Bridge.
properties.point_marks: Vauxhall Bridge. The works stood about half a mile (800 m) upstream of it; Snow gives the relation, not a position, and this point is not moved to guess one.

properties.name: Lambeth, to 1852 · Thames opposite Hungerford Market
properties.snow_says: The Lambeth Water Company continued to obtain their supply opposite to Hungerford Market; but they had established a small reservoir at Brixton.
properties.point_marks: Hungerford Bridge, which stands at the site of Hungerford Market. Snow says the supply was taken opposite the market, so the works were on the Lambeth bank.

properties.name: Lambeth, from 1852 · Thames at Thames Ditton
properties.snow_says: The Lambeth Company removed their water works, in 1852, from opposite Hungerford Market to Thames Ditton; thus obtaining a supply of water quite free from the sewage of London.
properties.point_marks: Thames Ditton village, the place Snow names. Secondary accounts put the new works at Seething Wells between Surbiton and Thames Ditton; this repository records Snow’s own words and does not adopt that refinement.

properties.name: Teddington Lock · the tidal limit of the Thames
properties.snow_says: the quantity of water which passes out to sea, with the ebb of every tide, is only equal to that which flows over Teddington Lock … so that the river becomes a kind of prolonged lake, the same water passing twice a day to and fro through London. [And, of the company:] Works are in progress for supplying a great part of London with water from the Thames, obtained, like that of the Lambeth Company, above Teddington Lock.
properties.point_marks: Teddington Lock, which SNOW HIMSELF names as the tidal boundary, twice. Below it the river is “a kind of prolonged lake, the same water passing twice a day to and fro through London”; above it only what flows over the lock reaches the sea. He also places the Lambeth Company’s supply above this lock by name, so the threshold, the company and which side it is on are all his.
